QF.id: AIFM CII Investment Landscape and Types_1

question.text: Mr. Ramesh Iyer keeps his salary surplus of INR 8 lakh in a savings bank account and a 3-month fixed deposit 'to use whenever I need cash'. He tells the AIF relationship manager of Lotus Capital AIF that he is 'actively investing' his money. From a Cat I/II AIF on-boarding standpoint, how should the Manager classify Mr. Iyer's current activity?

answer.text: It is saving, because funds are held in short-term liquid instruments without any defined time horizon or return objective.
It is investment, because parking money in any earning instrument is investment.
It is speculation, because short-term deposits involve uncertain interest rates.
It is alternative investment, because a savings bank pays interest above inflation.

explanation.text: The Logic: The chapter distinguishes saving from investment: saving is simply the difference between money earned and money spent, and savers typically park surpluses in short-term, highly liquid instruments (savings account, short-term FD, cash, gold) with no defined long-horizon goal. Investment is the current commitment of savings with an expectation of a higher amount over a specific time period. Mr. Iyer has no time-horizon or return objective, so he is saving, not investing. Every investor is a saver but not every saver is an investor. The Trap: (B) confuses an earning instrument with investment — the defining feature is a commitment over a specific horizon, not merely earning interest. (C) Speculation involves taking risk disproportionate to expected return without analysis — short-term FDs are not speculation. (D) A savings bank account is neither alternative nor a diversifier; alternatives are illiquid, private-market exposures. Cross-Exam Context: XIX-A (Cat I/II Distributor) tests the same saving-vs-investment distinction for client suitability. XXI-B (Portfolio Manager) treats it in the context of investment policy statements. X-A/X-B (Investment Adviser) covers it under client risk profiling. Manager's Pro-Tip: On a Cat I/II contribution agreement, the LP's risk profile must show genuine surplus that can be committed for 7-10 years (closed-end tenure). If a prospective LP's 'investment' surplus is actually the saving corpus for near-term needs, the capital commitment will likely default at drawdown. Screen this in the suitability section of the PPM.
